Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, the Awakened One, was the founder of Buddhism and one of history's most influential spiritual teachers. Born a prince in ancient Nepal around five hundred sixty-three BCE, he abandoned his palace to seek enlightenment and developed a path to liberation that has shaped the lives of over a billion people across Asia and the world. Siddhartha was born Prince Siddhartha of the Shakya clan in what is now Nepal, sheltered in luxury by his father until his encounter with human suffering at age twenty-nine. He renounced his princely life, wife, and child to become an ascetic wanderer, seeking to understand the nature of suffering and its cessation. After years of extreme austerity, he achieved Bodhi, awakening, beneath a Bodhi tree in Bodh Gaya, India, around five hundred twenty-eight BCE, becoming the Buddha. His core teachings, the Four Noble Truths, explain that suffering exists, has a cause in craving, can end, and can be ended through the Noble Eightfold Path. The concept of Dharma, universal law, and Karma, action and consequence, are central to Buddhist philosophy, emphasizing personal responsibility for one's spiritual path. Unlike contemporary traditions, he rejected the authority of the Vedas and the Brahmin priesthood, teaching that enlightenment is accessible to all regardless of caste. He established the Sangha, the monastic community of monks and nuns, creating institutional structures that preserved his teachings across centuries. Buddhism spread from India across Asia, developing into multiple schools and becoming one of the world's major religions.
